manoomin.askSay: (When you say yes, you offer Mishoomis one asemaa (tobacco).)

sugar_bush.name: Iskigamizigan
sugar_bush.note: 2026-10-08 (handoff/sugarbush_plan.md): sap, then syrup, then candy, each spring; the Quillwork makak the first time only

talk: Boozhoo, {name}. Sit by me. Can you smell it? Under the snow the ground is waking.
When the nights still freeze and the days begin to thaw, the ziinzibaakwadwaaboo (maple sap) runs. It is the first gift of the year, before the leaves, before anything else is green.
We go to the iskigamizigan (sugar bush) in the woods up the trail, where the ininaatig (maple) and the wiigwaasaatig (birch) stand together.

talk.*: You need something to catch it in. Migizi can fold you a biskitenaagan (birch bark sap bucket) from two sheets of wiigwaas (birch bark) and some ojiitad (sinew) - ask Ma'iingan for that. Or buy an akik (pail) at the store in Ashvale.
talk.ziibiing: You need something to catch it in. Migizi can fold you a biskitenaagan (birch bark sap bucket) from two sheets of wiigwaas (birch bark) and some ojiitad (sinew) - ask Ma'iingan for that.

talk: Each ininaatig gives once a day, and only on a day that thaws after a night that froze. Bring me one bucket of sap.
progress: One bucket of ziinzibaakwadwaaboo (maple sap), {name}. It runs only on a day that thaws after a night that froze, in the days before the maples bud. Ask Animikii what last night did.
complete: Miigwech (thank you), {name}. Taste it - it is only a little sweet, like water that remembers the tree.
It boils a long time before it is syrup. That is why we sit up all night by the akik (kettle).

talk.*: Now boil it. Any fire will do - ours here, one you light yourself, even Hob's range up in Ashvale - but watch it. Hang the akik from the iskigamiziganaak (kettle frame) and keep the fire high.
talk.ziibiing: Now boil it. Any fire will do - ours here, or one you light yourself - but watch it. Hang the akik from the iskigamiziganaak (kettle frame) and keep the fire high.

talk: When it is thick and gold, it is zhiiwaagamizigan (maple syrup). Bring me a bucket of it.
progress: A bucket of zhiiwaagamizigan (maple syrup), {name}. Boil your sap at a fire until it is thick and gold.
complete: Look at the colour of it. That is the colour of the sun in iskigamizige-giizis (the sugar-making moon).
One more boiling.

talk: Boil the syrup once more and stir it as it cools, and it sets into ziinzibaakwadoons (candy). The children wait all winter for it.
Bring me one piece. Your bucket will come back to you empty, ready for next spring.
progress: One piece of ziinzibaakwadoons (candy), {name}. Boil your syrup again at a fire.
complete: Ahh. That is the taste of the iskigamizigewigamig (sap-boiling lodge) when I was a little girl.

complete.*: I sewed this makak (birch bark box) for you this winter. Wiigwaas (birch bark), spruce root, and gaaway (porcupine quill) dyed for the flowers. Carry it on your back - it holds more than any pack the stone towns make.
complete.ziibiing: I sewed this makak (birch bark box) for you this winter. Wiigwaas (birch bark), spruce root, and gaaway (porcupine quill) dyed for the flowers. Carry it on your back - it holds more than any other pack.

complete: Come back to the iskigamizigan every spring, {name}. The trees will remember you.

again: Boozhoo, {name}! The nights are freezing and the days are thawing again. The ininaatig (maple) are ready.
Bring me a bucket of ziinzibaakwadwaaboo (maple sap), then syrup, then a piece of candy, as you did before.
done: Boozhoo, {name}. The sugar is put away in its makak for the year. Sit by the fire.
When the sap runs again next spring, come and find me.
notYet: The ziinzibaakwadwaaboo (maple sap) is not running yet. It runs when the nights still freeze and the days begin to thaw, before the ininaatig (maple) buds.
Come back {when}, and we will go up to the iskigamizigan (sugar camp) together.
askLackTalk: Come and sit by me, {name}. When you ask an elder to teach you, you bring a little asemaa (tobacco) - it is how we ask. Come back with some, and I will take you to the sugar bush.
sugar_bush.askLack: Bring asemaa (tobacco) to ask an elder for teaching.
sugar_bush.askSay: (When you say yes, you offer Nookomis one asemaa (tobacco).)

biiwaanag.name: Biiwaanag
biiwaanag.note: 2026-10-09 (handoff/ziibiing_bow_quests_plan.md): flint from the riverbank below the painted rock, a canoe trip down the river; a fire of your own

talk: Boozhoo, {name}. Sit. The fire in this wigwam was lit by my grandfather's hand, and it has never been let go out.
One of the people of Ziibiing (at the river) must be able to make a fire of their own. For that you need biiwaanag (flint).

Take the jiimaan (canoe) at the landing and paddle down the river, east, a little way. On the far bank, the south side, a rock face is painted with red figures. The bank under it is chalky, and biiwaanag (flint) lies in it. Pry it out with your fingers.
Here is a log from my woodpile. Lay it down, strike the biiwaanag (flint) over it until it catches, and come and tell me.
progress: A fire of your own, {name}. Biiwaanag (flint) lies in the chalky bank below the painted rock, down the river on the south side. Strike it over a log.
complete: I can smell the smoke on you. Good.
Keep the biiwaanag (flint). It does not wear out the way we do.

done: Boozhoo, {name}. Is your fire still going? Ishkode (fire) is a relative. Feed it and it looks after you.
askLackTalk: When you come to an elder for teaching, {name}, bring a little asemaa (tobacco). That is how it is done. Come back with some, and I will show you where the biiwaanag (flint) lies.
biiwaanag.askLack: Bring asemaa (tobacco) to ask an elder for teaching.
biiwaanag.askSay: (When you say yes, you offer Mishoomis one asemaa (tobacco).)

mitigwaab.name: Mitigwaab
mitigwaab.note: 2026-10-09: a maple log and ojiitad (sinew) for the bowstring, and a birch log for the arrows; two game hours later a maple bow (bound) and fifteen birch arrows; the tomahawk at the start

talk: Boozhoo, {name}. Ma'iingan tells me you snared a waabooz (rabbit) and earned your first ojiitad (sinew). Good. Now a mitigwaab (bow).
Take this tomahawk. It cuts wood, and it cuts the wiigwaas (birch bark) off a tree when you need some.

Bring me one log of ininaatig (maple) for the bow, your ojiitad (sinew) for the bowstring, and one log of wiigwaasaatig (birch) for the bikwak (arrows). The sugar bush up the trail is full of maple and birch.
Ininaatig (maple) is hard wood. Your arm is young, so it will take many swings. Keep at it.
progress: One ininaatig (maple) log, one ojiitad (sinew) and one wiigwaasaatig (birch) log, {name}. The sugar bush up the trail has the wood. The tomahawk will do it, slowly.
complete: Good wood, and good ojiitad (sinew). Feel the weight of that maple - it will bend for you and come back.

talk: Now leave me with it. A bow is shaved, not chopped, and the arrows want straightening over the fire.
Come back in two hours. Go and see Mishoomis, or cut yourself some wiigwaas (birch bark) with that tomahawk while you wait.
progress: Not yet, {name}. I am still working the bow. Come back a little later.
complete: Here. Your mitigwaab (bow), and fifteen bikwak (arrows) of birch.
They have no points. Birch is enough for a waawaashkeshi (deer) if the arrow finds it - two, and it is yours. Ma'iingan will want to see you hunt.
This bow was made for you. It will not go to anyone else.

done: Boozhoo, {name}. Bring me a wiigwaasaatig (birch) log whenever you need more bikwak (arrows).

deer_hunt.name: Waawaashkeshi
deer_hunt.note: 2026-10-09: with the bow, hunt a deer and bring its hide for sinew - the sinew for Migizi's birch bark sap bucket

talk: Boozhoo, {name}! Mitigwaabiike made you a mitigwaab (bow)? Then come hunting.
The waawaashkeshi (deer) graze in the open ground in the woods round the village. Go slowly. Two of the birch bikwak (arrows) bring one down, if they find it.
Bring me its hide, and I will give you ojiitad (sinew) from my rack. Migizi sews the sap buckets with it.
And cook the meat. Nobody hunts only for the hide.
progress: The hide of a waawaashkeshi (deer), {name}. The deer graze in the open ground in the woods. Two birch bikwak (arrows) bring one down.
complete: A good hide, cleanly taken. Miigwech (thank you).
Here, two lengths of ojiitad (sinew). Take them to Migizi with two sheets of wiigwaas (birch bark), and he will fold you a biskitenaagan (birch bark sap bucket) for the sugar bush.

done: Boozhoo, {name}. Any time you bring me the hide of a waawaashkeshi (deer), there is ojiitad (sinew) for you.

obsidian_arrows.name: Obsidian bikwak
obsidian_arrows.note: 2026-10-09: obsidian from the bank upriver by the cairn and a birch log; two game hours later fifteen obsidian-tipped arrows

talk: You have been shooting birch, {name}. Now I will show you a point.

Paddle up the river, west, on this side. A cairn of stones stands on the bank. Below it the bank is full of obsidian - black stone that breaks sharper than any knife. You need no pick; work it loose with your hands.
Bring me a piece of obsidian and another wiigwaasaatig (birch) log, and I will make you fifteen bikwak (arrows) with obsidian points.
progress: A piece of obsidian from below the cairn up the river, and a wiigwaasaatig (birch) log, {name}.
complete: Black as a winter night. Good.

talk: Knapping takes patience. Each point is struck a hundred times before it is sharp enough.
Come back in two hours and they will be ready.
progress: The points are not all knapped yet. Come back a little later, {name}.
complete: Fifteen obsidian bikwak (arrows). One of these brings down a waawaashkeshi (deer).
Whenever you need more, bring me the obsidian and the birch.

done: Boozhoo, {name}. Obsidian and birch, and I will make you more obsidian bikwak (arrows).

waabooz.name: Waabooz
waabooz.note: 2026-10-09: Ma'iingan lends a nagwaagan (snare); set it where the waabooz (rabbits) run, come back, and bring three pelts for your first ojiitad (sinew) - before the bow

talk: Boozhoo, {name}. You want a mitigwaab (bow)? Mitigwaabiike will want ojiitad (sinew) for the string, and you have none.
Before a hunter has a bow, he has a nagwaagan (snare). Here, take this one of mine.
Go where the waabooz (rabbits) run, in the brush round the village. Set it on the ground there and leave it. Come back in an hour or two and see what it holds.
Bring me three waabooz (rabbit) pelts, and I will give you your first ojiitad (sinew).
progress: Three waabooz (rabbit) pelts, {name}. Set the nagwaagan (snare) where they run, leave it, and come back to it later.
complete: Three pelts. Miigwech (thank you) - they will line a pair of makizinan (moccasins) for the winter.
Here is your ojiitad (sinew). Take it to Mitigwaabiike for a bowstring. Keep the nagwaagan (snare) - a hunter always has one set somewhere.

done: Boozhoo, {name}. Three waabooz (rabbit) pelts or one waawaashkeshiwayaan (deer hide), and I will give you ojiitad (sinew).
